title: AI tools for Forward Deployed Engineering — Vasuman Moza, Varick Agents

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: The talk's central subject is the three-stage forward deployed agent system (engagement agent, workflow agent, autonomous assistant) that structures how agents interact with enterprise workflows. The speaker describes the agent harness that works alongside Claude/Codex, how the engagement agent processes documentation and resolves entities, and how the autonomous assistant handles change requests. This is fundamentally about agent architecture and the control plane around models in an enterprise deployment context.

secondary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
secondary.rationale: Varick post-trains open-source models because frontier models are too verbose and lack the consultant's instinct for relevant detail. They build an RL environment with custom tools for reliable knowledge graph traversal, solving entity disambiguation and DAG violation detection. Post-training and RL are significant technical components of the talk.

secondary.label: Context Engineering & Memory
secondary.rationale: The dependency graph in Postgres as a single source of truth, entity disambiguation across enterprise systems, and context extraction from unstructured documentation (granola notes, Slack threads, PowerPoint) are fundamentally about what enters the model context and how state persists across the agent system.

secondary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
secondary.rationale: The FD agent platform (Varick OS) is infrastructure that forward deployed engineers build on—synthesizing engagement documentation, constructing workflows, and deploying agents. The platform is the substrate FDEs use, though it is more of an end-to-end system than pure developer tooling.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about enterprise operations automation: mapping department workflows, re-engineering processes around AI, deploying agents on top of existing systems of record (SAP, NetSuite, Salesforce), and delivering department-wide transformations with measurable ROI.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The FD agent platform serves as infrastructure that forward deployed engineers build on, similar to a developer platform for AI agent construction and deployment.

domains.label: Search & Knowledge
domains.rationale: Entity disambiguation, knowledge graph traversal, and context extraction from enterprise documentation (notes, Slack, PowerPoint) involve finding and resolving knowledge across heterogeneous sources.

summary: Vasuman Moza, CEO of Varick Agents, presents at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (San Francisco, June 30, 2026) on AI tooling for forward deployed engineers (FDEs). His central thesis: AI execution is no longer the bottleneck—models and harnesses have solved end-to-end execution of knowledge work. The remaining bottleneck is understanding each customer's unique business deeply enough to automate workflows end-to-end. Varick embeds FDEs with Fortune 500 enterprise clients to perform three core functions: (1) mapping how humans currently work by interviewing process leads and uncovering undocumented exceptions; (2) re-engineering processes around AI rather than applying AI to broken workflows; and (3) deploying agents on top of existing systems of record (SAP, NetSuite, Salesforce) without requiring migration—one client spent $5M and 5 years migrating to NetSuite with zero appetite for another. Varick delivers 25–75% department-wide ROI versus 5–10% from point solutions. JD Pruitt, head of engineering, details the FD agent platform with three stages: an engagement agent that synthesizes client documentation and resolves entity disambiguation; a workflow agent embedded alongside Claude or Codex to catch edge cases; and an autonomous assistant (in development) that processes client change requests without FDE involvement. The technical architecture uses a dependency graph in Postgres as a single source of truth, since enterprise workflows are remarkably linear despite cycles. Varick post-trains open-source models because frontier models are too verbose and lack the consultant's instinct for relevant detail. They also build an RL environment with custom tools for reliable knowledge graph traversal, solving problems like person disambiguation and DAG violation detection.
whyItMatters: The concepts in this talk form a coherent production system: forward deployed engineering defines the human workflow (audit/map → re-engineer → deploy on systems of record), the three-stage FD agent architecture amplifies each FDE's productivity across multiple concurrent client engagements, and the technical infrastructure—dependency graph in Postgres, post-trained open-source models for verbosity control, RL environment for reliable graph traversal, and entity disambiguation—makes the agents reliable enough for enterprise production. Together they explain why the bottleneck in enterprise AI has shifted from model execution to the human-intensive process of understanding each business deeply enough to automate it end-to-end, and how a purpose-built agent platform with custom post-trained models can scale that understanding where frontier models alone fail. The talk bridges software engineering practice (process re-engineering, systems integration, audit methodology) with AI engineering techniques (post-training, RL, knowledge graphs, agent orchestration) to solve a problem that neither discipline can address in isolation.
temporalContext: The talk was delivered on June 30, 2026, at the AI Engineer World's Fair in San Francisco and published on YouTube on July 28, 2026. By mid-2026, the enterprise AI landscape was grappling with the widely cited 'pilot purgatory' problem—95% of generative AI pilots failing to reach production and 87% producing no measurable ROI. The discourse had shifted from model capability (largely considered solved for knowledge work execution) to deployment and integration challenges. Forward deployed engineering as a practice was gaining significant attention, with companies like Cursor, Sierra, Decagon, and Ramp also presenting FDE-related talks at the same conference. The talk reflects a maturation in the AI engineering field: the bottleneck had moved from 'can models do this?' to 'can we deeply enough understand each enterprise's unique business to automate end-to-end workflows?' Varick Agents itself was a young company (founded January 2025) presenting early production results and an ambitious agent platform vision.
takeaways: AI execution is no longer the bottleneck; understanding each customer's unique business deeply enough to automate workflows end to end is the real bottleneck.
Varick delivers 25–75% department-wide ROI versus 5–10% from point solutions that only address one part of a process like prospecting or AP.

The FD agent platform has three stages: engagement agent (documentation synthesis and entity resolution), workflow agent (embedded in platform alongside Claude/Codex to catch edge cases), and autonomous assistant (in development for client change requests).
Varick uses a dependency graph in Postgres as a single source of truth, reflecting that enterprise workflows are remarkably linear despite containing cycles.

Frontier models are too verbose and lack the consultant's instinct for relevant detail; Varick post-trains open-source models to write normalized process flows with the right balance of detail and clarity.
An RL environment with custom tools trains models to traverse the knowledge graph reliably, solving problems like person disambiguation and DAG violation detection.
Every engagement begins with an audit (FDEs embedded to learn the company) followed by implementation, with the forward deployed motion—not technology—as the core bottleneck.
Enterprises are married to systems like SAP, NetSuite, and Salesforce—one client spent $5M and 5 years migrating to NetSuite and will not migrate again.
95% of generative AI pilots fail to reach production (MIT) and 87% produce no measurable ROI because AI is applied to broken processes rather than re-engineered workflows.

concepts.name: Entity Disambiguation
concepts.explanation: Resolving whether differently-spelled or similarly-named entities (e.g., multiple people named Mike, or Sarah spelled differently across email and Slack) across heterogeneous enterprise data sources refer to the same person. Frontier models like Claude handle this poorly, motivating post-trained models with graph-based tools.
concepts.importance: A core enterprise problem the FD agent platform solves; demonstrates a concrete use case where frontier models fail and post-trained models with custom graph-traversal tools succeed, justifying the entire post-training investment.

concepts.name: Post-Training Open-Source Models for Verbosity Control
concepts.explanation: Fine-tuning open-source models on domain-specific data to address frontier model limitations—specifically excessive verbosity and lack of consultant's instinct for what level of detail enterprise clients actually care about in normalized process flows.
concepts.importance: A key technical decision differentiating Varick's approach; explains why they maintain their own post-trained models rather than relying solely on frontier models, and the careers page confirms an active ML Engineer, Post Training role.

concepts.name: RL Environment for Knowledge Graph Traversal
concepts.explanation: A reinforcement learning environment with custom tools that trains models to reliably traverse a knowledge graph, solving problems like entity disambiguation, redundancy detection, and DAG violation identification that frontier models handle unreliably.
concepts.importance: Represents a novel application of RL to enterprise workflow analysis; demonstrates how custom tool environments can improve model reliability beyond what prompt engineering alone achieves.

concepts.name: Context Extraction from Unstructured Documentation
concepts.explanation: The engagement agent's ability to ingest unstructured enterprise documentation—meeting notes, Slack threads, PowerPoint slides—and produce structured workflow specifications with resolved entity references, converting tacit enterprise knowledge into machine-readable workflow representations.
concepts.importance: Addresses the fundamental challenge of making undocumented enterprise processes machine-readable; this is the input stage that feeds the dependency graph and enables all downstream agent stages.

concepts.name: Compound Agent Systems
concepts.explanation: Multi-step agent orchestration with retrieval, structured extraction, evaluation suites, and confidence-gated human-in-the-loop, as implemented in the Varick OS platform. The three-stage FD agent architecture is a production instance of this pattern.
concepts.importance: The architectural pattern underlying the entire FD agent system; represents a production-grade approach to enterprise agent deployment that goes beyond single-turn LLM interactions.

concepts.name: DAG Violation Detection
concepts.explanation: Identifying circular dependencies or redundant paths in workflow specifications represented as a directed acyclic graph, ensuring workflow structural correctness before deployment. The RL environment trains models to detect these violations reliably.
concepts.importance: A concrete validation step in the FD agent platform that ensures enterprise workflows are structurally sound before they are deployed to production systems of record.

concepts.name: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE)
concepts.explanation: A practice of embedding engineers within enterprise client teams to map current workflows, re-engineer processes around AI, and deploy agents on existing systems of record. Varick uses FDEs as the core delivery model for enterprise AI transformation, with every engagement beginning with an audit where FDEs learn the company from the inside out.
concepts.importance: Central organizing concept of the talk; defines the human role that the FD agent platform is designed to amplify, and frames the talk's thesis that the forward deployed motion—not technology—is the remaining bottleneck in enterprise AI.

concepts.name: Systems of Record Integration Without Migration
concepts.explanation: Building AI agents on top of existing enterprise systems (SAP, NetSuite, Salesforce, Dynamics, Workday) rather than requiring data migration, recognizing that enterprises have invested heavily in these systems and will not undertake another rip-and-replace cycle.
concepts.importance: Explains why Varick's approach is viable for enterprises locked into legacy infrastructure; the $5M/5-year NetSuite migration anecdote illustrates the prohibitive cost of alternative approaches.

concepts.name: Process Re-engineering Before AI Deployment
concepts.explanation: Redesigning business workflows around AI capabilities rather than applying AI to existing broken processes. FDEs decide which steps are fully automated, which need human-in-the-loop, and which remain human-operated, balancing ROI capture with user adoption.
concepts.importance: Explains why 95% of AI pilots fail to reach production and 87% produce no measurable ROI—AI applied to broken processes fails; re-engineering first is the prerequisite for production-grade enterprise AI.

concepts.name: Dependency Graph as Single Source of Truth
concepts.explanation: A Postgres-backed dependency graph representing enterprise workflows as a canonical data structure, exploiting the observation that enterprise workflows are remarkably linear despite containing cycles. Every agent stage reads from and writes to this graph.
concepts.importance: Provides the structural foundation for the entire FD agent platform; the graph enables entity disambiguation, DAG violation detection, and workflow validation across all three agent stages.

concepts.name: Three-Stage FD Agent Architecture
concepts.explanation: A staged agent system: (1) engagement agent that synthesizes documentation and resolves entity disambiguation; (2) workflow agent embedded alongside Claude/Codex to catch edge cases and ensure workflows correctly shadow the engineered process; (3) autonomous assistant (in development) that processes client change requests and ships workflow updates without FDE involvement.
concepts.importance: The core technical architecture presented in the talk; each stage amplifies FDE productivity at increasing levels of autonomy, culminating in a vision of fully autonomous workflow maintenance.

concepts.name: Varick OS Platform
concepts.explanation: The proprietary platform where all agents are spun up, monitored, optimized, and deployed. Includes runtime for long-running workflows against enterprise ERP/CRM environments, retrieval and context layer, eval and trace infrastructure, provider-agnostic model layer, and deployment tooling.
concepts.importance: The infrastructure substrate that makes the three-stage FD agent architecture possible; confirmed by first-party job postings detailing the full technical stack beyond what the transcript covers.

concepts.name: Audit-First Engagement Methodology
concepts.explanation: Every Varick engagement begins with an audit where FDEs and strategists embed with the client to learn the company from the inside out before any implementation begins, mapping real workflows versus documented SOPs.
concepts.importance: Defines Varick's go-to-market motion and explains why the forward deployed approach—not technology alone—is the core differentiator; the audit surfaces undocumented exceptions and handoffs that are the real bottleneck for autonomous AI.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop Workflow Design
concepts.explanation: During process re-engineering, FDEs explicitly categorize workflow steps as fully automated, human-in-the-loop, or fully human. The workflow agent flags ambiguous steps and edge cases for FDE review before deployment.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how Varick balances automation with reliability in enterprise settings where errors carry high cost; this graduated autonomy approach is key to achieving production-grade deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and the next bottleneck
sections.summary: Moza introduces Varick Agents and frames the talk around the next bottleneck: how deep can you go into a customer without scaling headcount exponentially, and how AI can do that job.

sections.title: Execution is no longer the bottleneck
sections.summary: AI has solved end-to-end execution of knowledge work. Models are intelligent enough and harnesses with browser use, API tooling, and MCPs enable near-perfect execution. The remaining bottleneck is understanding the business, since every company operates differently.

sections.title: What a forward deployed agent is — mapping current workflows
sections.summary: FDEs embed with a single department, interviewing process leads to understand how work runs today and what happens when things go wrong. The undocumented exceptions and handoffs are the real bottleneck for autonomous AI.

sections.title: Re-engineering processes around AI
sections.summary: AI fails when slapped onto broken processes. FDEs re-engineer workflows by deciding which steps are fully automated, which need human-in-the-loop, and which stay human, balancing ROI capture with user adoption.

sections.title: Deploying agents on top of existing systems
sections.summary: Enterprises are married to systems of record like NetSuite, SAP, Salesforce. Varick builds agents on top of these via their Varick OS platform with governance and eval suites, never asking clients to migrate.

sections.title: Why build the FDE agent
sections.summary: Top-1% FDEs with both technical depth and high EQ are extremely rare. The FDE agent amplifies each engineer to manage multiple client relationships, handling 24/7 communication and documentation. Knowledge work is nearly solved; designing work around AI is the next bottleneck.

sections.title: Department-wide ROI and introducing the FD agent platform
sections.summary: Moza contrasts point solutions (5–10% ROI for one part of a process) with Varick's department-wide transformations (25–75% ROI) across revenue uplift, cost savings, and risk mitigation. He introduces JD Pruitt, head of engineering, to explain the FD agent platform that amplifies FDE productivity.

sections.title: Three stages of the FD agent
sections.summary: JD Pruitt describes three stages: (1) engagement agent—an FDE assistant that pulls in granola notes, synthesizes documentation, reads PowerPoint slides, and resolves entity disambiguation questions; (2) workflow agent—embedded in the platform alongside Claude or Codex to catch edge cases and ensure workflows correctly shadow the engineered process; (3) autonomous assistant (in development)—processes client change requests and ships workflow updates without FDE involvement, freeing engineers for high-value client interviewing work.

sections.title: Technical architecture: dependency graph and post-trained models
sections.summary: The platform uses a dependency graph stored in Postgres as a single source of truth, since enterprise workflows are remarkably linear despite containing cycles. Varick post-trains open-source models because frontier models are too verbose and lack the consultant's instinct for what detail clients care about. They build an RL environment with custom tools for reliable knowledge graph traversal, solving problems like person disambiguation (multiple Mikes) and identifying redundancy or DAG violations.

sections.title: Closing: audit-first engagement and forward deployed motion
sections.summary: Moza closes by reiterating that Varick cannot be solved with just a product. Every engagement starts with an audit where FDEs and strategists learn the company from the inside out, followed by implementation. The forward deployed motion—not technology—is the core bottleneck. Varick is hiring aggressively and inviting interested enterprise clients to connect.

demonstrations: JD Pruitt demos the FD agent platform showing three stages: engagement agent (pulls granola notes, synthesizes docs, reads PowerPoint, resolves entity disambiguation), workflow agent (embedded in platform, works alongside Claude/Codex to flag edge cases), and autonomous assistant (in development, processes client change requests and ships workflow updates)
The engagement agent resolves questions like whether 'Sarah' spelled different ways in email and Slack are the same person
The workflow agent flags missing edge cases and prompts FDEs to verify process ownership before finalizing workflows

technologies.label: Varick OS Platform
technologies.summary: Varick OS is the proprietary agent platform built by Varick Agents where all agents are spun up, monitored, optimized, and deployed. It implements a three-stage FD agent architecture: (1) an engagement agent that synthesizes client documentation, reads PowerPoint slides, and resolves entity disambiguation questions like whether differently-spelled names refer to the same person; (2) a workflow agent embedded alongside Claude or Codex to catch edge cases and ensure constructed workflows correctly shadow the engineered process; and (3) an autonomous assistant (still in development) that processes client change requests and ships workflow updates without FDE involvement. First-party job postings confirm the platform includes runtime for long-running workflows against enterprise ERP/CRM environments, retrieval and context layer, eval and trace infrastructure, a provider-agnostic model layer, and compound agent systems with confidence-gated human-in-the-loop.
technologies.role: Primary platform technology; the talk's technical sections focus on its three-stage agent architecture, and JD Pruitt demos the platform showing the engagement agent resolving entity disambiguation and the workflow agent catching edge cases.

technologies.label: Dependency Graph in Postgres
technologies.summary: A dependency graph stored in Postgres serves as the single source of truth for enterprise workflows within the Varick OS platform. The speakers observe that enterprise workflows are remarkably linear despite containing cycles, making a graph representation tractable. Every agent stage reads from and writes to this graph. The graph enables entity disambiguation (resolving whether differently-spelled names across email, Slack, and documents refer to the same person), DAG violation detection (identifying circular dependencies or redundant paths), and workflow validation across all three agent stages.
technologies.role: Technical architecture foundation; discussed in the 'Technical architecture: dependency graph and post-trained models' section as the single source of truth that all agent stages depend on.

technologies.label: Post-Training Open-Source Models
technologies.summary: Varick post-trains open-source models because frontier models like Claude are too verbose and lack the consultant's instinct for what level of detail enterprise clients actually care about in normalized process flows. The post-trained models produce process flows with the right balance of detail and clarity. The Varick careers page confirms an active 'ML Engineer, Post Training' role, providing first-party evidence that post-training is an ongoing engineering function. The specific base model—reported as Qwen 2.5 by the secondary ZenML case study—remains unverified from first-party sources; the transcript refers only to 'open-source models.'
technologies.role: Explains why Varick maintains custom models rather than using frontier models for process analysis; discussed in the 'Technical architecture: dependency graph and post-trained models' section alongside the dependency graph.

technologies.label: RL Environment for Knowledge Graph Traversal
technologies.primary: RL Environment for Knowledge Graph Traversal
technologies.summary: Varick builds a reinforcement learning environment with custom tools for traversing their knowledge graph, training models to reliably solve problems that frontier models handle unreliably. These include person disambiguation (e.g., resolving whether multiple people named Mike across enterprise systems are the same person), redundancy detection, and DAG violation identification. The RL environment gives post-trained models the tool-use practice needed for reliable graph traversal in enterprise settings, bridging the gap between model capability and production reliability requirements.
technologies.role: Technical approach for making models reliable at graph traversal tasks; discussed alongside post-training in the 'Technical architecture' section as the solution to entity disambiguation and DAG violation problems.
